summary.text: Theophan is remembered as a bishop, translator, spiritual correspondent, and recluse. His withdrawal from public office follows years of teaching and episcopal service; it does not mean that he ceased helping people through letters and books.

blocks.text: Born George Govorov in a priest’s family, he studies at Kiev, receives monastic tonsure, and teaches in church schools. His service takes him to the Russian Mission in Jerusalem and the embassy church at Constantinople before he becomes bishop of Tambov.

blocks.text: The Holy Trinity account emphasizes his study of Greek and the Fathers during service in the Near East. It places the Russian Philokalia within that long preparation: the later translator had worked with the language and literature before retirement.

blocks.text: Transferred to Vladimir, he visits parishes, supports education, and shares the burdens of his flock. In 1866 he receives permission to retire to Vysha. From 1872 he lives in stricter reclusion while continuing extensive written counsel.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: The parish life distinguishes the first communal years at the monastery from the later reclusion. It describes a small cell, prayer, translation, and correspondence. These details identify one bishop’s particular vocation; they are a biographical account rather than a general instruction to isolate oneself.

blocks.text: The OCA describes weakening health in early 1894 and his peaceful death on January 6. His commemoration in this selected life is January 10. Neither date is automatically converted into a civil observance by this profile.

blocks.text: The parish source names the Philokalia, The Path to Salvation, letters, and Unseen Warfare. It explains that the last work passed from Lorenzo Scupoli through Nikodemos’s Greek adaptation to Theophan’s extensively revised Russian version. These are distinct editions; quotations from one translator should not be attributed to another.

blocks.title: Matthew 6:31–34
blocks.text:
Therefore take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or, What shall we drink? or, Wherewithal shall we be clothed?

(For after all these things do the Gentiles seek:) for your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things.

But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.

Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.

His pastoral correspondence means that reclusion and concern for others coexist in this biography. The source describes guidance offered across distance through letters, alongside translation and original writing. Published editions and translators remain identified when studying those works.
